latin.2175: XXVIII. Affine est quod legitur apud Alexandrum Morum de Victoria Gratiae, disputatione tertia thesi 15. Concedit enim posse dici hominem ante Gratiam habere potentiam quandam remotam & imperfectam ad opera pietatis & supernaturalia, modo per id designetur potentia naturalis volendi & nolendi quae proportionem atque adeo capacitatem homini conciliat, qualem nec in lapidibus reperias nec in brutis. Nempe id sibi vult, hominem, quantumlibet peccato corruptum, naturales quasdam facultates habere quae per Dei gratiam possunt ad pietatis opera moveri, quales facultates desunt in brutis atque inanimis. Et hoc est quod alii intelligunt per potentiam passivam & remotam. Nempe per istud significant hominem esse per naturam capacem recipiendorum gratiae divinae auxiliorum, per quae facultates ejus, novis viribus assumptis, ferantur in opera spiritualia atque salutaria.
latin.2176: XXIX. Josue Placaeus vero videtur aliquid amplius dicere, sed tamen quod eodem redit, quantum ad summam rei. Docet enim, quantacunque sit hominis corruptio, illum posse non peccare si vellet, & si ad non peccandum voluntas ejus esset, uti decet, comparata. Adeoque facultatem non peccandi in homine, si istud serio velit & ut oportet, non ascribendam esse gratiae, sed naturae. Affirmat enim eam facultatem etiam homini corrupto inesse, ut non modo peccare possit si velit, sed etiam non peccare, si quidem, uti par est, a peccato voluntas ejus abhorreret. Quare, inquit, non bene considerasse rerum naturas videntur illi qui facultatem non peccandi, si ad non peccandum, uti decet, comparata esset voluntas, gratiae tribuunt, cum sit potius ascribenda naturae, qua fit ut involuntarii & peccati rationes inter se pugnent. Unde colligit frustra nobis objici ea scripturae loca, quibus tribuit eam facultatem homini, ut possit bene agere si velit: nempe quomodo eum decet velle. Tractatu de libero arbitrio cap. 4.
latin.2177: XXX. Atque ut mentem suam clarius exponat vir ille Doctus, distinguit inter potentiam non peccandi & salutare bonum operandi conditionatam & absolutam. Potentiam non peccandi & bene operandi conditionatam vocat, per quam homo non peccare & bene operari potest si velit, & modo velit, sicut ipsum velle par est. Absolutam vero potentiam vocat, per quam homo simpliciter potest non peccare, & bene agere.
latin.2178: XXXI. Rursus potentia ista absoluta ab eo distinguitur in primam & secundam. Prima ab ipso vocatur ipsa naturalis facultas, per quam homo capax est bene & male agendi, quod brutis non convenit. Potentia absoluta bene agendi quam secundam vocat, consistit in habitibus potentiam naturalem ad bene agendum determinantibus, sive inclinantibus.
latin.2179: XXXII. Cum autem in actione morali discerni possit materia seu substantia actionis a forma, hoc est bonitate vel malitia morali, dicit potentiam primam esse principium materiale actionum moralium, secundam vero principium formale. Quoniam a voluntate, quae est potentia naturalis, per quam bene vel male agere possumus, est ipsum velle: ab habitibus vero voluntatem inclinantibus vel determinantibus, est bene vel male velle.
latin.2180: XXXIII. Quibus positis, affirmat in nobis per peccatum corruptis esse potentiam primam, sive principium materiale tam bene quam male agendi, sed amissam esse per peccatum Adami potentiam secundam, sive principium formale bene agendi, nec amissam modo, sed in contrariam potentiam conversam, ut ad id quod demum est bene agere secundum Deum, in omnibus nostris facultatibus moralibus insit universalis repugnantia, eo tenacior quod & ab ipso ortu insita est, & perpetua consuetudine, quasi altera natura, confirmata.
latin.2181: XXXIV. Eodem refertur alia distinctio qua utitur idem Placeus, & cum eo alii plurimi. Hic enim distinguunt inter potentiam sive impotentiam Physicam, & Moralem. Impotentia Physica ad bene agendum est, cum potentia naturalis intelligendi & volendi, sine qua nemo vel bene vel male agere potest, aut deest aut sui compos non est: Impotentia vero moralis est, quum mens quidem & voluntas adest, & est etiam sui compos, sed per habitus quosdam ad male agendum determinata est. Vel ut aliis verbis rem eandem explicat Placeus impotentia Physica est quae posita est extra voluntatem, hoc est per quam rem non potes, quantumlibet velis & coneris. Impotentia vero moralis est quae sita est in ipsa voluntate, hoc est, per quam non potes aliquid quia non vis, & habitu firmo ac penitus inhaerente ad oppositum voluntas tua determinata est. Qualis impotentia cernitur in daemonibus respectu amoris in Deum. Etenim Deum amare non possunt, non quod iis desit ulla facultas naturalis necessaria ad Deum amandum, sed quia propria & libera voluntate in Dei odio prorsus obfirmati sunt.
latin.2182: XXXV. Jam vero docent illi Theologi hominem etiam peccato corruptum, absque ulla gratia inhaerente sive subjectiva, habere quandam potentiam Physicam sive naturalem ad opera pietatis, quatenus nulla deest ipsi facultas naturalis necessaria ad opera istiusmodi obeunda, nec etiam ullo Physico impedimento prohibetur, quominus illis vacet; veruntamen illum moraliter ad ista opera omnino impotentem esse, quia naturales illius facultates, mens scilicet & voluntas, habitibus vitiosis ita obsitae & praepeditae sunt, ut nihil in hoc genere, sine gratia sanante & liberante possit.
latin.2183: XXXVI. Sunt quidem inter Reformatos qui distinctionem istam improbare videntur, ut inter alios Alexander Morus. Nam impotentiam hominis ad bonum existimat Physicam esse & dici debere, quoniam nobis innata est, & in nos cum ipsa natura propagatur: eandem vero incaute moralem appellari, quia in usu communi illud Moraliter impossibile dicimus, non quod simpliciter fieri non potest, sed quod solum difficillimum est atque vix, aegre, & raro fit. Itaque mavult, quod ad hanc quaestionem attinet, impotentiam hominis distingui in eam quae est involuntaria, & extrinsecus accersita, aut profecta ab infirmitate: & in eam quae interna & voluntaria est, & proficiscitur a malignitate, non ab infirmitate. Ad quod posterius genus revocat impotentiam quae homini tribuitur respectu boni salutaris. De Victoria Gratiae Disput. 6. Thesi 13.
latin.2184: XXXVII. Sed qui aliter in hac materia loquuntur, non aliud tamen sentiunt. Nam impotentiam hominis circa bonum spirituale ideo moralem vocant, quia voluntaria est, & a vitio profecta: non quod putent in hoc genere hominem ex se posse quicquam facere vel conari, licet aegre, rarissime atque difficillime. Et ultro etiam concedunt talem impotentiam homini a primo ortu insitam esse, eamque propterea solum Physicam dici nolunt, quia non procedit ex carentia potentiae seu facultatis alicujus naturalis, sed tantum ex vitiosa & culpabili ejus corruptione: quod alii minime negant: adeoque hic est merum inter Reformatos de vocibus certamen.
latin.2185: XXXVIII. Caeterum quamvis passim doceant Protestantes hominem in prima sui conversione mere passive se habere, mens tamen eorum non est primos actus quibus homo ad Deum convertitur, incipiendo peccatum odisse atque detestari, & Deum amare ac illi credere & fidere, non esse actus vitales, a facultatibus hominis elicitos, ac proinde active ab eo procedentes: Sed illud solum sibi volunt, gratiam Dei nostram voluntatem praevenire, & voluntatem nostram mere passive se habere respectu primorum illorum auxiliorum, quibus Deus voluntatem nostram ad bonum movere incipit, & novarum illarum virium quas Deus illi gratuito infundit, & sine quibus nihil boni incipere, vel conari, nec etiam gratiae divinae cooperari potest.
latin.2186: XXXIX. Id sedulo monet Perkinsus. Dicimus, inquit, in prima peccatoris conversione liberum hominis arbitrium cum gratia certa quadam ratione concurrere, velut socium ac cooperans. Ad conversionem enim tria requiruntur: verbum, Spiritus Sanctus & voluntas hominis. Nam voluntas hominis non est saltem & omnimodo passiva; sed est etiam ipsius quaedam operatio, etiam in prima animae conversione. Etenim quum quis convertitur, fit id quidem a Deo; verum hominem non cogente invitum, sed ita voluntatem ejus inclinante, ut etiam ipse homo conversionem suam velit. Nam quum jam homo convertitur, vult etiam ipse ex Dei gratia suam conversionem. Et postea quibusdam subjunctis, Meminisse debemus, inquit, quod etiam in ipso primo momento conversionis, operatio gratiae Spiritus Sancti, ac voluntas hominis desiderans eam, in homine simul fiunt: hoc tamen discrimine, quod operatio Spiritus Sancti, quantum ad ordinem & causam attinet, prior est, ac voluntatem movet & excitat: haec vero mota & ad agendum excitata a gratia, deinceps seipsam quoque movet & operatur. In Catholico Reformato Controv. 1. cap. 1. Conclusione 5.
latin.2187: XL. Et eodem quoque redit doctrina Theologorum confessionis Augustanae. Quod Lutherus, inquiunt, scripsit hominis voluntatem in conversione pure passive se habere, id recte & dextre est accipiendum, videlicet, respectu divinae gratiae in accendendis novis motibus: hoc est, de eo intelligi oportet, quando spiritus Dei per verbum auditum, aut per usum Sacramentorum hominis voluntatem aggreditur, & conversionem atque regenerationem in homine operatur. Postquam enim Spiritus Sanctus hoc ipsum jam operatus est, atque effecit, hominisque voluntatem sola sua divina virtute & operatione immutavit atque renovavit: tunc revera hominis nova illa voluntas instrumentum est & organum Dei Spiritus Sancti, ut ea non modo gratiam apprehendat, verum etiam in operibus sequentibus Spiritui Sancto cooperetur. In Epitome articulorum de quibus controversiae ortae sunt inter Theologos Confessionis Augustanae art. 2. qui est de libero arbitrio.
latin.2188: XLI. Quod idem postea confirmant in solida ac perspicua repetitione & declaratione quorundam articulorum Augustanae Confessionis, de quibus aliquandiu inter nonnullos Theologos eidem addictos disputatum fuit, quae ut praecedens Epitome inserta est libro Concordiae. Quando, inquiunt, Lutherus affirmat hominem in conversione sua pure passive se habere, id est, plane nihil agere, sed tantummodo pati id quod Deus in ipso agit, certe non sentit quod conversio absque praedicatione & auditione verbi Dei fiat: neque haec ita accipi voluit, quasi in conversione per Spiritum Sanctum prorsus nulli novi motus in nobis excitentur, neque ulla spiritualis operatio in nobis inchoetur, sed hoc voluit Lutherus, hominem ex seipso aut naturalibus suis viribus non posse aliquid conferre, vel adjumentum adferre ad suam conversionem: & hominis conversionem non tantum ex parte, sed totam prorsus esse operationem, donum, & opus solius Spiritus Sancti.
latin.2189: XLII. Et tamen eo non obstante, censent iidem Theologi hominis conversionem ita liberam esse, ut homo possit Spiritui Sancto conversionis opus in nobis aggredienti resistere, & obicem ponere, imo & de facto quandoque resistat & obicem ponat: nec ullam esse Spiritus Sancti efficaciam, quam homo pertinacia & contumacia sua, fructu & effectu suo frustrari non valeat. Huc tendit quod affirmant Theologi Rintelenses in suo Colloquio cum Marpurgensibus, Cassellis authoritate Hassiae Landgravii habito. Etenim ad quaestionem illam, An Gratia conversionis ita se habeat, ut homo in virtute gratiae Evangelio obsequium praestare, & per connatam malitiam ei resistere, & obicem ponere aeque possit? Affirmative respondent, negantibus Marpurgensibus.
latin.2190: XLIII. Etsi vero negent Reformati gratiam per quam Deus homines ad se convertit, talem esse, ut homo quandoque obicem illi ponat, & effectum ejus impediat; & pertendant nunquam contingere, ut Deo conversionis opus aggredienti, homo sic resistat, ut inconversus maneat; quoniam gratiae divinae efficacia tanta est in homine peccatore, ut conversionem ejus operetur infallibiliter & insuperabiliter: fatentur tamen efficaciam illam non obstare, quominus hominis conversio sit opus vere liberum, & quod ab homine non solum active sed etiam libere procedit: quia, scilicet, gratia divina, quantumlibet per se efficax, hominem tamen non movet, nisi ut creaturae Rationali & liberae congruum & consentaneum est. Nempe praestat infallibiliter non solum ut homo faciat & velit, sed ut libere faciat & velit, & ut in operibus bonis, ad quae gratia illum movet, non minus agat ex proprio judicio, electione, & deliberatione, ac si sine gratia ageret.
latin.2191: XLIV. Quinimo quamvis pertendant, posita gratia per quam Deus homines convertit, fieri non posse quin conversio sequatur; nec simul stare posse gratiae convertentis motum atque impulsum, & talem voluntatis humanae resistentiam, quae conversionis actum impediat: attamen agnoscunt simul cum efficacia gratiae consistere potentiam ad actum oppositum, & negationem actus ad quem gratia hominem impellit. Nempe hominem, etsi convertatur infallibiliter, semper retinere veram potentiam se non convertendi, & contrarium actum eliciendi.
latin.2192: XLV. Id expresse docet Amesius in Bellarmino Enervato. Nam explicans quo sensu homo per praevenientem gratiam excitatus & a Deo adjutus, ita valeat operari, ut possit etiam non operari, observat istud posse operari & non operari, posse dupliciter exponi: primo ut sensus sit, quod potentia ad non operandum sit simul in eodem subjecto cum gratia, & auxilio quod requiritur ad operandum, & hunc sensum dicit esse verissimum. Secundo modo dicta verba sic intelligi posse, ut sensus sit quod gratia, & auxilium ad talem operationem particularem datum, & carentia talis actus, seu actus contrarius aliquando simul sint, aut esse possint in eodem subjecto: quem sensum dicit esse falsum.
latin.2193: XLVI. Ideoque ad quaestionem An homines per liberum arbitrium agant in operibus pietatis, Respondet, si phrasis illa agere per liberum arbitrium, significat liberum arbitrium in istis operibus agere ut principium quod, illam a nobis admitti: si vero significet libertatem naturalem esse principium quo actionis spiritualis, non vero accipere & posse & velle suum a gratia, eam a nobis rejici tanquam Pelagianam. Lib. 4. de Libr. Arbitr. cap. 3. de viribus liberi arbitrii.
latin.2194: XLVII. Porro ex iis quae hactenus exposita sunt patet Protestantes non negare, post peccatum & ante gratiam, homini inesse potentiam quandam remotam & imperfectam ad opera pietatis & supernaturalia. Et hoc nomine illos designare facultatem naturalem volendi & nolendi, quae respectu istorum operum proportionem quandam & capacitatem homini conciliat, qualis nec in lapidibus, nec in brutis reperitur.
latin.2195: XLVIII. Praeterea eosdem fateri potentiam istam in homine post peccatum residuam, respectu eorundem operum liberam esse, non tantum a coactione, sed etiam ab omni Physica necessitate, & determinatione bruta. Unde est quod eorum multi dicere non verentur, hominem ante gratiam potentiam Physicam habere salutare bonum operandi, illumque posse bene operari si velit, licet ad hoc sit moraliter impotens, propter voluntatem ejus pravis habitibus in malo obfirmatam.
latin.2196: XLIX. Ex dictis quoque planum est, Protestantes agnoscere liberum arbitrium, quod post peccatum in homine mansit, esse principium quod, aut ut alii dicunt, materiale actionum piarum & spiritualium, licet ante gratiam careat illa libertate, quae est principium quo sive formale actionum illarum. Liberum vero arbitrium, recuperata illa bene agendi libertate, per auxilia gratiae a Deo subministrata, cooperari divinae gratiae, non solum in actibus primam conversionem hominis sequentibus, verum etiam in iis in quibus prima illa conversio consistit. Ac proinde Protestantes eosdem non negare quin omnia bona hominis opera, quae gratiae tribuenda sunt, active & libere ab hominis voluntate, quam gratia movet & excitat, procedant: adeoque quin homo sibi innata & essentiali libertate utatur, sive dum actus ipsi in Evangelio praeceptos, propria impulsus malitia, omittit, sive dum illos, gratia auxiliante, elicit.
latin.2197: L. Nec minus clarum fecimus Confessionis Augustanae Doctores eam libertatem homini tribuere, per quam divinae gratiae effectum, non tantum impedire possit, sed de facto saepe impediat: Reformatos vero docere gratiam quidem liberum hominis arbitrium ad bene agendum movere atque determinare infallibiliter & insuperabiliter, sed propterea tamen ab eo non tollere veram potentiam aliter agendi, & ab actione cessandi: ita ut homo posita gratia, non possit illi dissentire, ut Scholae loquuntur in sensu composito, possit tamen in sensu diviso.
latin.2198: LI. Ex quibus omnibus evidenter sequitur, Bellarminum & alios Scholae Romanae Doctores frustra disputare contra Protestantes, quasi negarent simpliciter hominem in sua conversione cooperari divinae gratiae, & conversionem ipsam esse opus liberum, & quod homo, divina gratia movente & excitante, libere eliciat. Ac plane nullum & falso positum esse statum controversiae, quem constituit Bellarminus inter Protestantes omnes & Ecclesiam Romanam. An scilicet, homo post peccatum, ita sit liberi arbitrii in iis rebus quae pertinent ad salutem, ut quamvis nihil possit sine auxilio gratiae, tamen per gratiam praevenientem excitatus & a Deo adjutus, ita valeat operari, ut possit etiam non operari?
latin.2199: LII. Nam inter Protestantes collective consideratos, & Scholam Romanam etiam collective consideratam, nulla prorsus est ea de re controversia, quanquam in utraque Schola disputetur inter Theologos, quo sensu homo, posita gratia, possit operari & non operari. Sunt enim in Schola Romana plurimi qui, positis quibusvis gratiae auxiliis, volunt hominem sic posse bene operari, & non operari, ut id verum sit etiam in sensu composito, non solum in sensu diviso: hoc est, qui volunt nulla esse gratiae auxilia, quorum effectum homo contumacia sua aliquando non impediat, & effectu suo frustretur: Et inter Protestantes plurimi quoque idem sentiunt atque profitentur, nempe omnes Theologi Confessionis Augustanae, & etiam qui Remonstrantes dicuntur. Ac quemadmodum in eo ab iis dissentiunt qui singulariter dicuntur Reformati, quorum doctrina est, omnia gratiae auxilia ad actualem hominis conversionem necessaria & praerequisita nunquam suo effectu carere, sed omnem cordis humani contumaciam & resistentiam infallibiliter ab illis superari: sic quoque in Schola Romana reperiuntur non pauci qui idem, quoad summam rei, cum Reformatis hac in parte sentiunt, & dissident a reliquis Scholae Romanae Theologis; Ac docent gratiam divinam sic per se efficacem esse, ut liberum hominis peccatoris arbitrium ad bonum determinet indeclinabiliter & insuperabiliter, quamvis ab eo non tollat potestatem dissentiendi, & aliter agendi. Quo de numero sunt non tantum Jansenius & ejus discipuli, sed etiam qui dicuntur Thomistae recentiores, ut Didacus Alvares, & Gulielmus Estius.
latin.2200: LIII. Vicissim vero manifestum fecimus Scholae Romanae Theologos cum Protestantibus fateri liberum hominis arbitrium, ante gratiam, sic esse peccati servum, ut nihil possit in iis in quibus vera & salutifera pietas in Deum consistit. Imo primum initium justificationis & conversionis nostrae a solo Deo esse, non vero a nostro libero arbitrio, & eo respectu hominem mere passive se habere.
latin.2201: LIV. Nec minus clarum est ex dictis Ecclesiae Romanae Doctores, ut Bellarminum, & Molinam ipsum, quod liberum arbitrium gratiae cooperatur, non tribuere naturae viribus, sed novis illis quas voluntas nostra per auxilium gratiae accepit. Nec eorum mentem esse, liberum arbitrium quum gratiae consentit, & ductum illius sequitur, id facere per vires quas jam ante habebat, & quarum solummodo usus impediebatur, antequam esset per gratiam solutum, quod suis falso imponi queritur Bellarminus, sed per vires quas Deus ipsi supra naturam addidit: ita ut consensus quem voluntas hominis gratiae vocanti & excitanti praebet, sit opus non naturale, sed supernaturale.
latin.2202: LV. Proinde fatendum est inter Protestantes & Ecclesiam Romanam non esse hic eum quem ponit Perkinsus controversiae statum. An, scilicet, voluntas hominis naturalem potentiam habeat cooperandi gratiae divinae in rebus spiritualibus, quod dicit affirmari ab Ecclesiae Romanae Doctoribus, a nostris vero negari; quia juxta nos quod voluntas cooperatur, habet a gratia; at juxta Scholae Romanae Doctores a seipsa. Dicunt, inquit, voluntatem hominis concurrere & cooperari gratiae Dei in prima conversione hominis peccatoris per seipsam, & naturali quadam sua potentia, eamque solum a Spiritu Sancto juvari. At nos dicimus, cooperari quidem gratiae voluntatem hominis in prima conversione; sed non a seipsa motam, sed a gratia: a qua necesse est prius moveatur & erigatur, antequam seipsam movere, aut quicquam bene velle possit. Qua in re falli Perkinsum manifestum est ex iis quae supra retulimus: cum expresse doceant Doctores Scholae Romanae voluntatem humanam gratiae cooperari, non per vires proprias, sed per eas quas ipsi gratia de novo suffecit. In Catholico Reformato Contr. 1. cap. 2.
latin.2203: LVI. At, inquies, quid ergo illud est de quo contenditur inter Protestantes & Scholam Romanam, dum haec quidem affirmat hominem ante gratiam arbitrii sui libertatem habere, non solum ad opera naturalia & moralia, sed etiam ad opera pietatis & supernaturalia: illi vero istud negant. Respondeo, multos quidem ex Doctoribus Ecclesiae Romanae variis modis nimium tribuere libero arbitrio, ut superioribus disputationibus a nobis ostensum est: sed quod ad hanc praecise quaestionem attinet, videri certamen esse de vocibus.
latin.2204: LVII. Nam dum negant Protestantes hominem ante gratiam libertatem suam habere, quantum spectat ad opera spiritualia & supernaturalia, per id negare non intendunt hominem ante gratiam praeditum esse ea libertate, quae voluntati essentialis est, & quae opponitur necessitati Physicae & brutae determinationi, etiam circa res spirituales & supernaturales: adeoque hominem in eo statu libere omittere actus supernaturales in Evangelio praeceptos; quum vero per gratiam movetur, iisdem actibus libere defungi, & sic aut aliter agendi, saltem in sensu diviso, veram potestatem habeat: sed illud solum sibi volunt hominem in eo statu non esse liberum a servitute peccati, & a dependentia motionis divinae per auxilium supernaturale, & sine tali auxilio, in negotio salutis eum nihil omnino posse. Quum vero Schola Romana affirmat hominem ante gratiam liberum esse in rebus spiritualibus & quae ad pietatem spectant, per id inficiari non vult hominem ante gratiam esse peccati servum, & nihil prorsus eum sine gratia posse, in iis in quibus vera erga Deum pietas consistit. Sed mens ejus solum est, hominem per naturam talem esse, & ea essentiali libertate praeditum, ut gratia auxiliante libere in bonum feratur, & veram semper potestatem habeat illud faciendi, aut non faciendi.
latin.2205: LVIII. Similiter quum dicunt Protestantes liberum arbitrium in homine per peccatum extinctum & amissum esse, non vero simpliciter sauciatum & attenuatum, respectu boni salutaris atque spiritualis, illud tantum sibi volunt, nullas in homine post peccatum superesse vires quibus ex se in bonum feratur, sed quicquid in salutis aeternae negotio potest & operatur, nulla ex parte tribui debere propriis liberi arbitrii viribus, sed solum illis quas de novo Christi gratia ei suppeditavit. Quum vero contra Scholae Romanae Theologi contendunt liberum hominis arbitrium non esse penitus amissum, sed tantum captivatum, ligatum, & vulneratum, etiam in iis quae salutem aeternam hominis promovent, per id significare nolunt, liberum hominis peccatoris arbitrium in operibus piis atque salutiferis, aliquid licet aegre & difficulter sine gratia posse: imo nequidem docere intendunt hominem per gratiam excitatum & adjutum, & quasi vinculis solutum, propriis viribus illi cooperari, non autem per novas vires quas gratia superaddit: sed hoc duntaxat sibi volunt, naturalem hominis libertatem circa nullum objectum per peccatum amissam esse, sed tantum hominis mentem & voluntatem pravis qualitatibus per peccatum inductis impediri, ne, sicut oportet, ferantur in verum & salutare bonum: adeo ut opus non sit facultates illas de novo nobis dare, & novum quoddam liberum arbitrium in nobis creare, sed solum mentem atque voluntatem a vulneribus peccati sanare, & novis viribus additis auxilio gratiae juvare, ad hoc ut bene agere possimus.
latin.2206: LIX. A quo non abludit doctrina Reformatorum supra exposita, juxta quam statuunt omnes potentias Physicas necessarias ad bene agendum, quae non aliud sunt quam ipsum liberum arbitrium absolute consideratum, in homine post peccatum remansisse, & solum per peccatum inductam esse quandam impotentiam moralem, quae tota consistat in pravis habitibus mentem & voluntatem ita obsidentibus, ut bonum salutare nec agnoscere, nec amare possint, aut vel tantillum se ad illud promovere, donec iis per Christi gratiam liberentur. Ex quibus omnibus patet, Protestantes Scholae Romanae quidem verbis contradicere, sed reipsa tamen non negare quod Schola Romana affirmare intendit, & sic, ut jam diximus, non de re ipsa, sed de verbis hic contentionem esse.
latin.2207: LX. Nec tamen loquendi modus quo utuntur Protestantes, dum aiunt hominem per peccatum amisisse arbitrii libertatem, ad verum & salutare bonum, sic universim in Schola Romana improbatur, quin viri in ea & celebres & docti agnoscant illum ex Augustino desumptum, & scripturae ac veteris Ecclesiae stylo consentaneum esse. Quod bona fide fatentur Jansenius & ejus Discipuli, ut supra a nobis ostensum.

sections.title: Alexander Morus: a remote and imperfect power means only the natural capacity of willing
sections.pass_a: XXVIII. Akin is what is read in Alexander Morus On the Victory of Grace, the third disputation, thesis 15. For he grants that it can be said that man before Grace has a certain remote and imperfect power for works of piety and supernatural ones, provided that by it is designated the natural power of willing and nilling which procures for man a proportion and so a capacity, such as you would find neither in stones nor in brutes. Namely he means this, that man, however much corrupted by sin, has certain natural faculties which through the grace of God can be moved to the works of piety, such faculties as are lacking in brutes and inanimate things. And this is what others understand by a passive and remote power. Namely by that they signify that man is by nature capable of receiving the helps of divine grace, through which his faculties, new strength being taken on, may be borne to spiritual and saving works.
pass_b: Close to this is a passage in Alexander Morus, De Victoria Gratiae, disputation 3, thesis 15. He allows that man before grace may be said to have a remote and imperfect power for works of piety and supernatural works, so long as that phrase means the natural power of willing and refusing. That power gives man a proportion to such works and so a capacity for them, which you would not find in stones or in beasts.

His point is that man, however corrupted by sin, has natural faculties that God's grace can move to works of piety; beasts and lifeless things have no such faculties. Others mean the same by a passive and remote power: man is by nature able to receive the helps of divine grace, and through them his faculties take on new strength and move toward spiritual and saving works.

sections.title: Placaeus: fallen man could not sin if he willed as he ought, so the power not to sin belongs to nature
sections.pass_a: XXIX. But Josué de la Place seems to say something more, but yet what comes to the same thing, as to the sum of the matter. For he teaches that, however great the corruption of man may be, he could not sin if he willed, and if his will were disposed for not sinning, as is fitting. And so that the faculty of not sinning in man, if he wills it seriously and as he ought, is to be ascribed not to grace, but to nature. For he affirms that faculty to be in man even corrupt, so that not only can he sin if he will, but also not sin, if indeed, as is right, his will shrank from sin. Wherefore, he says, those seem not to have considered well the natures of things who attribute to grace the faculty of not sinning, if the will were disposed for not sinning as is fitting, since it is rather to be ascribed to nature, by which it comes about that the notions of the involuntary and of sin conflict with each other. Whence he gathers that those places of scripture are objected to us in vain, which attribute that faculty to man, that he can act well if he will: namely in the way it befits him to will. Treatise on free choice, chapter 4.
pass_b: Josué de la Place seems to go further, though in substance he arrives at the same place. However deep man's corruption, he teaches, man could avoid sin if he willed to, that is, if his will were set against sinning as it ought to be. So the ability not to sin, given a serious and proper willing, is to be credited to nature and not to grace.

He holds that even corrupt man has this ability: he can sin if he wishes, and he can also not sin, provided his will recoils from sin as it should. 'So,' he says, 'those who credit grace with the ability not to sin, on the condition that the will were rightly set against sinning, seem not to have weighed the nature of things well. It belongs rather to nature, which makes the notions of the involuntary and of sin conflict with each other.'
From this he concludes that it is useless to cite against us the scriptures that grant man the ability to do good if he wills, meaning if he wills as he should. Treatise on free choice, chapter 4.

sections.title: Placaeus distinguishes conditional and absolute power not to sin
sections.pass_a: XXX. And that that learned man may set forth his mind more clearly, he distinguishes between a conditional and an absolute power of not sinning and of working saving good. The conditional power of not sinning and of working well he calls that by which man can not sin and work well if he will, and provided he will, as it is right that he should will. But the absolute power he calls that by which man can simply not sin, and act well.
pass_b: To make his meaning plainer, that learned man separates a conditional from an absolute power of not sinning and of doing saving good.

The conditional power is the one by which a man is able to refrain from sin and do good if he wills, and on condition that he wills as he ought. The absolute power is the one by which a man simply is able to refrain from sin and to act well.

sections.pass_a: XXXI. Again that absolute power is distinguished by him into first and second. The first is called by him the natural faculty itself, by which man is capable of acting well and ill, which does not belong to brutes. The absolute power of acting well which he calls second, consists in habits determining, or inclining, the natural power to acting well.
pass_b: He divides this absolute power further into a first and a second. The first is simply the natural faculty that makes man able to act well or badly, something beasts do not have. The second absolute power of acting well consists in habits that determine or incline the natural power toward acting well.

sections.title: The first power is the material principle of moral acts, the second the formal
sections.pass_a: XXXII. But since in a moral action the matter or substance of the action can be distinguished from the form, that is, the moral goodness or badness, he says that the first power is the material principle of moral actions, but the second the formal principle. Since from the will, which is the natural power by which we can act well or ill, is willing itself: but from the habits inclining or determining the will, is willing well or ill.
pass_b: In a moral action one can tell apart its matter or substance from its form, which is its moral goodness or badness. Accordingly he calls the first power the material principle of moral actions and the second the formal principle.
The bare act of willing comes from the will, the natural power by which we are able to act well or badly; willing well or willing badly comes from the habits that incline or determine the will.

sections.title: In fallen man the first power remains, the second is lost and turned into its contrary
sections.pass_a: XXXIII. Which things being laid down, he affirms that in us, corrupted through sin, there is the first power, or material principle of acting both well and ill, but that through the sin of Adam the second power, or formal principle of acting well, was lost, and not only lost, but turned into a contrary power, so that toward that which in the end is to act well according to God, there is in all our moral faculties a universal repugnance, the more tenacious because it is both implanted from our very birth, and confirmed by perpetual custom, as a second nature.
pass_b: On these premises he holds that in us, corrupted by sin, the first power remains, the material principle of acting either well or badly. The second power, the formal principle of acting well, was lost through Adam's sin.

It was not merely lost but changed into the opposite power. So all our moral faculties carry a universal resistance to the one thing that finally is acting well according to God, and it is all the more stubborn because it is ingrained from birth and reinforced by constant habit, like a second nature.

sections.title: Physical and moral inability (Placaeus); the demons cannot love God
sections.pass_a: XXXIV. To the same is referred another distinction which the same Placaeus uses, and with him very many others. For here they distinguish between Physical and Moral power or inability. Physical inability for acting well is when the natural power of understanding and willing, without which no one can act either well or ill, either is lacking or is not master of itself: But moral inability is when the mind and will are indeed present, and are also masters of themselves, but are determined through certain habits to acting ill. Or as Placaeus explains the same thing in other words, Physical inability is that which is placed outside the will, that is, through which you cannot do a thing, however much you will and try. But moral inability is that which is situated in the will itself, that is, through which you cannot do something because you will not, and your will is determined to the opposite by a firm and deeply inhering habit. Such inability is seen in the demons in respect of love toward God. For they cannot love God, not because they lack any natural faculty necessary for loving God, but because by their own and free will they are wholly hardened in hatred of God.
pass_b: Another distinction belongs here, used by Placaeus and many others with him: physical power or inability against moral. Physical inability to act well exists when the natural power of understanding and willing, without which nobody can act either well or badly, is absent or not in its own control.

Moral inability exists when mind and will are present and in their own control, but have been fixed by certain habits on acting badly. Placaeus also puts it another way. Physical inability lies outside the will: it is what keeps you from doing a thing however much you want and try. Moral inability lies in the will itself: you cannot do something because you do not want to, your will being fixed on the opposite by a firm and deep-rooted habit.

This is the inability we see in the demons with respect to loving God. They cannot love God, not for want of any natural faculty needed to love him, but because of their own free will they are entirely hardened in hatred of God.

sections.title: Fallen man has physical power for works of piety but is morally unable without healing grace
sections.pass_a: XXXV. Now those Theologians teach that man, even corrupted by sin, without any inherent or subjective grace, has a certain Physical or natural power for the works of piety, inasmuch as no natural faculty necessary for performing works of that kind is lacking to him, nor is he prevented by any Physical impediment from giving himself to them; but nevertheless that he is morally wholly unable for those works, because his natural faculties, namely mind and will, are so beset and hindered by vicious habits, that he can do nothing in this kind without healing and freeing grace.
pass_b: These theologians teach that man, even corrupted by sin and lacking any inherent or subjective grace, has a physical or natural power for works of piety. He lacks no natural faculty needed to perform such works, and no physical obstacle keeps him from attending to them.

Yet morally he is wholly unable to do them, because his natural faculties, mind and will, are so hemmed in and obstructed by vicious habits that he can do nothing of this kind without grace that heals and sets free.

sections.title: Morus rejects the distinction: man's inability is physical, better called voluntary and malign
sections.pass_a: XXXVI. There are indeed among the Reformed those who seem to disapprove that distinction, as among others Alexander Morus. For he thinks that man's inability for good is Physical and ought to be so called, since it is innate in us, and is propagated into us with nature itself: but that the same is incautiously called moral, because in common usage we call that Morally impossible, not which simply cannot be done, but which is only most difficult and is done scarcely, hardly, and rarely. And so he prefers, as regards this question, that man's inability be distinguished into that which is involuntary, and brought in from outside, or proceeding from weakness: and into that which is internal and voluntary, and proceeds from malignity, not from weakness. To which latter kind he refers the inability which is attributed to man in respect of saving good. On the Victory of Grace Disputation 6. Thesis 13.
pass_b: Some of the Reformed, however, seem to reject this distinction, Alexander Morus among others. He judges that man's inability for good is physical and should be called so, since it is born in us and passes into us together with our nature.

Calling it moral is careless, in his view, because in ordinary speech 'morally impossible' means not what simply cannot be done but only what is extremely hard and happens scarcely, with difficulty and seldom.

On this question he would rather divide man's inability into two kinds. One is involuntary, brought in from outside, or arising from weakness; the other is inward and voluntary and arises from malice, not weakness. To the second kind he assigns the inability ascribed to man regarding saving good. De Victoria Gratiae, disputation 6, thesis 13.

sections.title: Those who speak otherwise mean the same: a mere dispute about words
sections.pass_a: XXXVII. But those who speak otherwise in this matter, do not yet think otherwise. For they call man's inability about spiritual good moral for this reason, because it is voluntary, and proceeds from vice: not because they think that in this kind man of himself can do or attempt anything, though hardly, most rarely and most difficultly. And they also freely grant that such inability is implanted in man from his first birth, and they refuse to call it Physical for this reason only, because it does not proceed from the lack of any natural power or faculty, but only from its vicious and culpable corruption: which the others by no means deny: and so here there is a mere contest of words among the Reformed.
pass_b: Those who use different language here do not hold a different view. They call man's inability regarding spiritual good moral because it is voluntary and comes from vice, not because they think that man can do or even attempt anything of this kind by himself, however hard, rare and difficult the attempt.

They readily grant that this inability is ingrained in man from birth. Their only reason for not calling it physical is that it does not come from the lack of some natural power or faculty but solely from that faculty's vicious and blameworthy corruption, which the others do not deny at all. Among the Reformed, then, this is purely a quarrel over words.

sections.title: Passivity in conversion concerns only the first helps and new strength, not the acts of conversion
sections.pass_a: XXXVIII. Moreover although the Protestants everywhere teach that man in his first conversion behaves merely passively, yet their mind is not that the first acts by which man is converted to God, by beginning to hate and detest sin, and to love God and to believe and trust in him, are not vital acts, elicited by the faculties of man, and so proceeding actively from him: But they mean only this, that the grace of God goes before our will, and that our will behaves merely passively in respect of those first helps, by which God begins to move our will to good, and of those new strengths which God freely pours into it, and without which it can begin nothing good, or attempt it, nor even cooperate with divine grace.
pass_b: The Protestants commonly teach that man is merely passive in his first conversion. They do not mean that the first acts by which a man turns to God, beginning to hate and loathe sin, to love God and to believe and trust him, are not living acts produced by man's faculties and so coming actively from him.

They mean only that God's grace goes ahead of our will, and that our will is merely passive with respect to the first helps by which God begins to move it toward good, and with respect to the new strengths God pours into it freely. Without these it cannot begin or attempt anything good, nor even cooperate with divine grace.

sections.title: Perkins: in the first conversion the will concurs with grace as a companion
sections.pass_a: XXXIX. This Perkins carefully warns. We say, he says, that in the first conversion of the sinner the free choice of man concurs with grace in a certain way, as a companion and cooperating. For three things are required for conversion: the word, the Holy Spirit and the will of man. For the will of man is not at least and in every way passive; but there is also a certain operation of it, even in the first conversion of the soul. For when anyone is converted, it is done indeed by God; but not compelling man unwilling, but so inclining his will, that man himself also wills his conversion. For when man is now converted, he himself also wills his conversion out of the grace of God. And afterwards, certain things being added, We ought to remember, he says, that even in the very first moment of conversion, the operation of the grace of the Holy Spirit, and the will of man desiring it, take place in man together: yet with this difference, that the operation of the Holy Spirit, as regards order and cause, is prior, and moves and arouses the will: but this, moved and aroused to act by grace, thereafter also moves itself and works. In the Reformed Catholic Controversy 1. chapter 1. Conclusion 5.
pass_b: Perkins takes care to make this point. 'We say,' he writes, 'that in the sinner's first conversion man's free choice concurs with grace in a certain way, as a partner and a co-worker. Three things are needed for conversion: the word, the Holy Spirit and man's will. Man's will is not simply and in every respect passive; it has some working of its own, even in the soul's first conversion.

When anyone is converted, God does it, but not by forcing an unwilling man; he so inclines his will that the man himself wills his own conversion. For when a man is being converted, he too wills his conversion, by the grace of God.'

A little later he adds: 'We must remember that even at the very first moment of conversion the working of the Holy Spirit's grace and man's will that desires it occur in man together. The difference is that the Spirit's working comes first in order and as cause, and moves and rouses the will; the will, once moved and roused to act by grace, then also moves itself and works.' The Reformed Catholic, controversy 1, chapter 1, conclusion 5.

sections.title: The Lutheran Epitome: Luther's 'purely passive' concerns the kindling of new motions
sections.pass_a: XL. And to the same also comes the doctrine of the Theologians of the Augsburg confession. That Luther, they say, wrote that the will of man in conversion behaves purely passively, is to be taken rightly and properly, namely, in respect of divine grace in kindling new motions: that is, it must be understood of when the spirit of God, through the word heard, or through the use of the Sacraments, approaches the will of man, and works conversion and regeneration in man. For after the Holy Spirit has already wrought and effected this very thing, and has changed and renewed the will of man by his divine power and operation alone: then truly that new will of man is the instrument and organ of God the Holy Spirit, so that by it not only does he apprehend grace, but also in the following works cooperates with the Holy Spirit. In the Epitome of the articles about which controversies arose among the Theologians of the Augsburg Confession art. 2. which is on free choice.
pass_b: The teaching of the theologians of the Augsburg Confession comes to the same thing. 'Luther's statement,' they say, 'that man's will is purely passive in conversion must be taken in the right and proper sense: with respect to divine grace kindling new motions. It refers to the moment when God's Spirit, through the word heard or the use of the sacraments, takes hold of man's will and works conversion and regeneration in him.

Once the Holy Spirit has done and accomplished this, and has changed and renewed man's will by his divine power and working alone, then man's new will really is an instrument and organ of God the Holy Spirit: so that it not only lays hold of grace but also cooperates with the Holy Spirit in the works that follow.' Epitome of the articles in controversy among the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, article 2, on free choice.

sections.title: The Solid Declaration explains Luther: conversion wholly the work of the Spirit, not without the word
sections.pass_a: XLI. Which the same afterwards confirm in the solid and clear repetition and declaration of certain articles of the Augsburg Confession, about which there was for some time dispute among certain Theologians devoted to it, which like the preceding Epitome is inserted in the book of Concord. When, they say, Luther affirms that man in his conversion behaves purely passively, that is, does nothing at all, but only suffers what God works in him, he certainly does not think that conversion takes place without the preaching and hearing of the word of God: nor did he wish these things to be so taken, as if in conversion through the Holy Spirit no new motions at all were aroused in us, nor any spiritual operation begun in us, but Luther meant this, that man of himself or by his natural strength cannot confer anything, or bring help to his conversion: and that the conversion of man is not only in part, but wholly and entirely the operation, gift, and work of the Holy Spirit alone.
pass_b: They confirm the same afterwards in the Solid Declaration, a full and clear restatement of certain articles of the Augsburg Confession that had for a time been disputed among some theologians who adhered to it; like the Epitome before it, this is included in the Book of Concord.

'When Luther affirms,' they say, 'that man is purely passive in his conversion, that is, does nothing at all but only undergoes what God works in him, he certainly does not think conversion happens without the preaching and hearing of God's word. Nor did he want this taken as if in conversion the Holy Spirit stirred up no new motions in us at all and began no spiritual working in us.

What Luther meant is that man cannot contribute anything, or bring any help to his conversion, of himself or by his natural powers; and that man's conversion is not partly but entirely the working, gift and work of the Holy Spirit alone.'

sections.title: The Lutherans hold conversion resistible (the Rinteln-Marburg colloquy at Kassel)
sections.pass_a: XLII. And yet notwithstanding this, the same Theologians judge the conversion of man to be so free, that man can resist the Holy Spirit undertaking the work of conversion in us, and put an obstacle, nay and in fact sometimes resists and puts an obstacle: and that there is no efficacy of the Holy Spirit which man by his obstinacy and contumacy is not able to frustrate of its fruit and effect. Hither tends what the Rinteln Theologians affirm in their Colloquy with those of Marburg, held at Kassel by the authority of the Landgrave of Hesse. For to that question, Whether the Grace of conversion is such that man in the strength of grace can equally render obedience to the Gospel, and through innate malice resist it, and put an obstacle? They answer affirmatively, those of Marburg denying.
pass_b: Even so, the same theologians hold that man's conversion is free in such a way that a man can resist the Holy Spirit as he sets about the work of conversion in us, and can put an obstacle in his way; indeed sometimes a man actually does resist and obstruct. There is no efficacy of the Holy Spirit, on their view, that a man cannot by his stubbornness and defiance rob of its fruit and effect.

This is the drift of what the Rinteln theologians affirm in their colloquy with the Marburg theologians, held at Kassel by the authority of the Landgrave of Hesse. To the question 'Is the grace of conversion such that a man, by the strength of grace, can equally obey the Gospel and, through inborn malice, resist it and put an obstacle in its way?' they answered yes; the Marburg side said no.

sections.title: The Reformed: grace converts infallibly, yet conversion is a truly free work
sections.pass_a: XLIII. But although the Reformed deny that the grace by which God converts men to himself is such that man sometimes puts an obstacle to it, and hinders its effect; and maintain that it never happens that, when God undertakes the work of conversion, man so resists that he remains unconverted; since the efficacy of divine grace is so great in the sinful man, that it works his conversion infallibly and insuperably: yet they confess that that efficacy does not prevent the conversion of man from being a truly free work, and one which proceeds from man not only actively but also freely: because, namely, divine grace, however efficacious of itself, yet does not move man, except as is suitable and agreeable to a Rational and free creature. Namely it brings about infallibly not only that man does and wills, but that he freely does and wills, and that in the good works to which grace moves him, he acts no less from his own judgment, choice, and deliberation, than if he were acting without grace.
pass_b: The Reformed deny that the grace by which God turns men to himself is such that a man may sometimes block it and prevent its effect. They maintain that when God takes up the work of conversion it never happens that a man resists so as to stay unconverted, because divine grace is so powerful in the sinner that it brings about his conversion infallibly and irresistibly.

Yet they admit that this power does not stop man's conversion from being a truly free work, one that comes from the man not only actively but freely. The reason is that divine grace, however effective in itself, moves a man only in a way that suits and fits a rational and free creature.

It infallibly secures not just that the man acts and wills but that he acts and wills freely, so that in the good works to which grace moves him he acts from his own judgement, choice and deliberation no less than if he were acting without grace.

sections.title: The Reformed admit a true power of not converting, alongside efficacious grace
sections.pass_a: XLIV. Nay although they maintain that, grace being posited by which God converts men, it cannot happen that conversion does not follow; nor can there stand together the motion and impulse of converting grace, and such resistance of the human will as would hinder the act of conversion: yet they acknowledge that together with the efficacy of grace there subsists a power for the opposite act, and for the negation of the act to which grace impels man. Namely that man, although he is converted infallibly, always retains a true power of not converting himself, and of eliciting the contrary act.
pass_b: They do maintain that once the grace by which God converts men is given, conversion cannot fail to follow, and that the motion and push of converting grace cannot coexist with a resistance of the human will strong enough to block the act of conversion.

Still they recognize that, together with the efficacy of grace, a power remains for the opposite act and for not performing the act grace drives a man to. A man who is converted infallibly still always keeps a real power not to turn himself and to produce the contrary act.

sections.title: Ames on 'able to work and not to work': true in one sense, false in the other
sections.pass_a: XLV. This Ames expressly teaches in Bellarmine Disarmed. For explaining in what sense man, aroused by prevenient grace and helped by God, is so able to work, that he can also not work, he observes that this, can work and not work, can be expounded in two ways: first so that the sense is, that the power for not working is at the same time in the same subject with grace, and the help which is required for working, and this sense he says is most true. In the second way the said words can be so understood, that the sense is that grace, and the help given for such a particular operation, and the lack of such an act, or the contrary act, are sometimes at the same time, or can be in the same subject: which sense he says is false.
pass_b: Ames teaches this plainly in his Bellarminus Enervatus. Explaining the sense in which man, roused by prevenient grace and helped by God, can act in such a way that he can also not act, he notes that 'can act and not act' may be read in two ways.

In the first reading, the power not to act exists in the same subject at the same time as grace and the help needed for acting; this sense, he says, is entirely true. In the second reading, grace and the help given for a particular act, together with the absence of that act or the contrary act, sometimes exist or can exist in the same subject at once; this sense, he says, is false.

Book 4. on Free Choice chap. 3. on the strength of free choice.
pass_b: So when asked whether men act through free choice in works of piety, he answers as follows. If 'acting through free choice' means that free choice acts in those works as the principle that acts (principium quod), we accept it.

If it means that natural freedom is the principle by which (principium quo) a spiritual action is done, and does not receive both its ability and its willing from grace, we reject it as Pelagian. Book 4, on free choice, chapter 3, on the powers of free choice.

Moreover that the same confess that that power remaining in man after sin is free in respect of the same works, not only from coaction, but also from every Physical necessity, and brute determination. Whence it is that many of them are not afraid to say, that man before grace has the Physical power of working saving good, and that he can work well if he will, although for this he is morally unable, on account of his will hardened in evil by depraved habits.
pass_b: They also grant that the power left in man after sin is free with respect to those works, not only from compulsion but from all physical necessity and brute determination.

That is why many of them do not hesitate to say that man before grace has a physical power to do saving good and can do good if he wills, though he is morally unable to do it because his will is hardened in evil by perverse habits.

sections.title: Free choice is the material principle of pious acts; freed by grace it cooperates even in first conversion
sections.pass_a: XLIX. From what has been said it is also plain, that the Protestants acknowledge that free choice, which remained in man after sin, is the principle which, or as others say, the material principle of pious and spiritual actions, although before grace it lacks that freedom, which is the principle by which or formal principle of those actions. But that free choice, that freedom of acting well being recovered, through the helps of grace supplied by God, cooperates with divine grace, not only in the acts following the first conversion of man, but also in those in which that first conversion consists. And therefore the Protestants do not deny that all the good works of man, which are to be attributed to grace, proceed actively and freely from the will of man, which grace moves and arouses: and so that man uses his innate and essential freedom, whether when, impelled by his own malice, he omits the acts prescribed to him in the Gospel, or when, grace helping, he elicits them.
pass_b: What has been said also makes clear that the Protestants recognize free choice, which survived in man after sin, as the principle that acts (principium quod), or as others put it the material principle, of pious and spiritual actions. Before grace, however, it lacks the freedom that is the principle by which (principium quo), the formal principle of those actions.

Once that freedom to act well has been regained through the helps of grace God supplies, free choice cooperates with divine grace, not only in the acts that follow a man's first conversion but in the very acts that make up that first conversion.

So the Protestants do not deny that all of man's good works, which must be credited to grace, come actively and freely from man's will as grace moves and rouses it. Nor do they deny that man uses his inborn and essential freedom both when, driven by his own malice, he leaves undone the acts the Gospel commands him, and when, with grace helping, he performs them.

sections.title: Lutherans: man can and does hinder grace; Reformed: grace determines infallibly, yet in the divided sense he can dissent
sections.pass_a: L. pass_b: We have shown just as clearly that the doctors of the Augsburg Confession ascribe to man a freedom by which he is able not only to hinder the effect of divine grace but often does hinder it in fact.

The Reformed teach instead that grace moves and determines man's free choice to act well infallibly and irresistibly, yet does not for that reason remove its real power to act otherwise and to stop acting. Given grace, then, a man cannot dissent from it in what the Schools call the composite sense, though he can in the divided sense.

sections.title: Bellarmine's state of the controversy is falsely laid down
sections.pass_a: LI. From all which it evidently follows, that Bellarmine and other Doctors of the Roman School dispute in vain against the Protestants, as if they simply denied that man in his conversion cooperates with divine grace, and that conversion itself is a free work, and one which man, divine grace moving and arousing, freely elicits. And that the state of the controversy which Bellarmine constitutes between all the Protestants and the Roman Church is plainly null and falsely laid down. Namely, Whether man after sin is so of free choice in those things which pertain to salvation, that although he can do nothing without the help of grace, yet aroused by prevenient grace and helped by God, he is so able to work, that he can also not work?
pass_b: All this plainly shows that Bellarmine and other doctors of the Roman School argue against the Protestants to no purpose, as though the Protestants flatly denied that man cooperates with divine grace in his conversion, and that conversion itself is a free work that man performs freely as divine grace moves and rouses him.

It also shows that the state of the question Bellarmine sets up between all Protestants and the Roman Church is empty and falsely stated. His question is: 'After sin, does man have free choice in matters of salvation in such a way that, though he can do nothing without the help of grace, yet when roused by prevenient grace and helped by God he can act in such a way that he can also not act?'

sections.title: No controversy between the two sides taken collectively; the divide runs through each school
sections.pass_a: LII. For between the Protestants considered collectively, and the Roman School also considered collectively, there is no controversy at all on that matter, although in both Schools it is disputed among the Theologians, in what sense man, grace being posited, can work and not work. For there are in the Roman School very many who, any helps of grace whatever being posited, will that man can so work well, and not work, that this is true also in the composite sense, not only in the divided sense: that is, who will that there are no helps of grace, whose effect man by his contumacy does not sometimes hinder, and frustrate of its effect: And among the Protestants very many also think and profess the same, namely all the Theologians of the Augsburg Confession, and also those who are called Remonstrants. And as in this those dissent from them who are called Reformed in particular, whose doctrine is, that all the helps of grace necessary and prerequisite for the actual conversion of man never lack their effect, but that all the contumacy and resistance of the human heart is infallibly overcome by them: so also in the Roman School are found not a few who think the same, as to the sum of the matter, with the Reformed in this part, and dissent from the other Theologians of the Roman School; And teach that divine grace is so efficacious of itself, that it determines the free choice of sinful man to good indeclinably and insuperably, although it does not take from it the power of dissenting, and of acting otherwise. Of which number are not only Jansenius and his disciples, but also those who are called the more recent Thomists, as Diego Alvarez, and William Estius.
pass_b: Between the Protestants taken as a whole and the Roman School taken as a whole there is no dispute at all on this point, although within each school theologians argue over the sense in which man, once grace is given, can act and not act.

Many in the Roman School hold that, whatever helps of grace are given, man can act well and not act in such a way that this is true in the composite sense too, not only in the divided sense. In other words, there is no help of grace whose effect a man may not sometimes block by his defiance and frustrate. Many Protestants hold and profess the same: all the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, and also those called Remonstrants.

Those specifically called Reformed disagree with them here. Their doctrine is that every help of grace necessary and prerequisite for a man's actual conversion always takes effect, and that it infallibly overcomes all the defiance and resistance of the human heart.

In the same way the Roman School has not a few who agree with the Reformed on this point in substance and part company with the other Roman theologians. They teach that divine grace is so effective in itself that it determines the sinner's free choice to good unswervingly and irresistibly, though it does not take away his power to dissent and act otherwise. Among them are not only Jansenius and his disciples but also the so-called later Thomists, such as Diego Alvarez and William Estius.

sections.pass_a: LIII. Nay that the first beginning of our justification and conversion is from God alone, not from our free choice, and in that respect man behaves merely passively.
pass_b: Conversely, we have shown that the theologians of the Roman School admit with the Protestants that man's free choice before grace is so enslaved to sin that it can do nothing in the things that make up true and saving piety toward God.
They even admit that the very beginning of our justification and conversion comes from God alone and not from our free choice, and that in this respect man is merely passive.

sections.title: Bellarmine and Molina ascribe cooperation not to nature but to new supernatural strength
sections.pass_a: LIV. Nor is it less clear from what has been said that the Doctors of the Roman Church, as Bellarmine, and Molina himself, do not attribute it to the strength of nature that free choice cooperates with grace, but to those new strengths which our will has received through the help of grace. Nor is it their mind, that free choice when it consents to grace, and follows its leading, does it through strength which it had already before, and whose use only was hindered, before it was loosed through grace, which Bellarmine complains is falsely imputed to his own, but through strength which God has added to it above nature: so that the consent which the will of man gives to grace calling and arousing, is a work not natural, but supernatural.
pass_b: What has been said makes it just as clear that the doctors of the Roman Church, Bellarmine and Molina himself among them, credit free choice's cooperation with grace not to the powers of nature but to the new powers our will has received through the help of grace.

They do not mean that free choice, when it consents to grace and follows its lead, does so by powers it already had, whose use was merely blocked until grace set it loose; Bellarmine complains that this is falsely charged against his side. They mean it does so by powers God has added to it beyond nature, so that the consent man's will gives to grace as it calls and rouses is a supernatural work, not a natural one.

sections.title: Perkins's state of the controversy is also mistaken
sections.pass_a: LV. Therefore it must be confessed that between the Protestants and the Roman Church that is not the state of the controversy here which Perkins lays down. Namely, Whether the will of man has a natural power of cooperating with divine grace in spiritual things, which he says is affirmed by the Doctors of the Roman Church, but denied by ours; because according to us what the will cooperates, it has from grace; but according to the Doctors of the Roman School from itself. They say, he says, that the will of man concurs and cooperates with the grace of God in the first conversion of the sinful man by itself, and by a certain natural power of its own, and that it is only helped by the Holy Spirit. But we say, that the will of man cooperates indeed with grace in the first conversion; but not moved by itself, but by grace: by which it must first be moved and raised up, before it can move itself, or will anything well. In which matter it is manifest that Perkins is deceived from those things which we reported above: since the Doctors of the Roman School expressly teach that the human will cooperates with grace, not through its own strength, but through that which grace has newly supplied to it. In the Reformed Catholic Contr. 1. chap. 2.
pass_b: We must therefore admit that the state of the question between the Protestants and the Roman Church is not the one Perkins sets out here: whether man's will has a natural power to cooperate with divine grace in spiritual things. He says the doctors of the Roman Church affirm this and ours deny it, because on our view the will has its cooperation from grace, and on the Roman doctors' view from itself.

'They say,' he writes, 'that man's will concurs and cooperates with God's grace in the sinner's first conversion by itself and by some natural power of its own, and is only helped by the Holy Spirit. We say that man's will does cooperate with grace in the first conversion, but not as moved by itself; it is moved by grace, which must first move and lift it up before it can move itself or will anything well.'

What we reported above makes clear that Perkins is mistaken here, since the doctors of the Roman School teach expressly that the human will cooperates with grace not by its own powers but by those grace has newly supplied to it. The Reformed Catholic, controversy 1, chapter 2.

sections.title: What each side means by affirming or denying freedom before grace
sections.pass_a: LVII. For while the Protestants deny that man before grace has his freedom, as far as regards spiritual and supernatural works, by that they do not intend to deny that man before grace is endowed with that freedom, which is essential to the will, and which is opposed to Physical necessity and brute determination, even about spiritual and supernatural things: and so that man in that state freely omits the supernatural acts prescribed in the Gospel; but when he is moved through grace, freely performs the same acts, and has a true power of acting so or otherwise, at least in the divided sense: but they mean only this, that man in that state is not free from the servitude of sin, and from dependence on the divine motion through supernatural help, and that without such help, in the business of salvation he can do nothing at all. But when the Roman School affirms that man before grace is free in spiritual things and those which regard piety, by that it does not wish to deny that man before grace is the slave of sin, and that he can do nothing at all without grace, in those things in which true piety toward God consists. But its mind only is, that man is by nature such, and endowed with that essential freedom, that, grace helping, he is freely borne to good, and always has a true power of doing it, or of not doing it.
pass_b: When the Protestants deny that man before grace has his freedom with respect to spiritual and supernatural works, they do not mean to deny that man before grace has the freedom essential to the will, opposed to physical necessity and brute determination, even regarding spiritual and supernatural things.

So they allow that man in that state leaves undone freely the supernatural acts the Gospel commands; and that when grace moves him he performs those acts freely and has a real power to act one way or the other, at least in the divided sense. All they mean is that man in that state is not free from bondage to sin or from dependence on God's motion through supernatural help, and that without such help he can do nothing whatever in the matter of salvation.

When the Roman School, for its part, affirms that man before grace is free in spiritual things and things of piety, it does not mean to deny that man before grace is a slave of sin and can do nothing at all without grace in the things that make up true piety toward God. It means only that man is by nature so made, and so endowed with that essential freedom, that with grace helping he moves freely toward good and always has a real power to do it or not do it.

sections.title: Likewise 'extinguished' and 'wounded' mean the same in substance
sections.pass_a: LVIII. Similarly when the Protestants say that free choice in man has been extinguished and lost through sin, and not simply wounded and weakened, in respect of saving and spiritual good, they mean only this, that no strengths remain in man after sin by which of himself he may be borne to good, but that whatever he can do and works in the business of eternal salvation, ought in no part to be attributed to the proper strength of free choice, but only to those which the grace of Christ has newly supplied to it. But when on the other hand the Theologians of the Roman School contend that the free choice of man is not wholly lost, but only made captive, bound, and wounded, even in those things which promote the eternal salvation of man, by that they do not wish to signify, that the free choice of sinful man in pious and salutary works, can do something, though hardly and with difficulty, without grace: nay they do not even intend to teach that man aroused and helped by grace, and as it were loosed from chains, cooperates with it by his own strength, and not by the new strength which grace superadds: but they mean only this, that the natural freedom of man has been lost through sin about no object, but only that the mind and will of man are hindered by depraved qualities brought in through sin, so that they are not borne, as they ought, to true and saving good: so that there is no need for those faculties to be given to us anew, and for some new free choice to be created in us, but only that the mind and will be healed of the wounds of sin, and be helped by the help of grace, new strength being added, to this end that we may act well.
pass_b: In the same way, when the Protestants say that man's free choice was extinguished and lost through sin, not simply wounded and weakened, with respect to saving and spiritual good, they mean only that after sin no strength is left in man by which he could move toward good of himself. Whatever he is able to do and does in the matter of eternal salvation must not be credited in any part to free choice's own powers, but only to those Christ's grace has newly supplied.

When the theologians of the Roman School, on the other side, contend that man's free choice is not wholly lost but only taken captive, bound and wounded, even in what furthers man's eternal salvation, they do not mean that a sinner's free choice can do anything in pious and saving works without grace, even with difficulty and effort.

They do not even mean to teach that man, roused and helped by grace and as it were freed from chains, cooperates with grace by his own powers rather than by the new powers grace adds. Their meaning is only this: man's natural freedom was lost through sin with respect to no object at all. What happened is that his mind and will are obstructed by perverse qualities sin brought in, so that they do not move toward true and saving good as they should.

On this view those faculties need not be given to us afresh, nor a new free choice created in us. Mind and will need only to be healed of the wounds of sin and helped by grace with new strength added, so that we can act well.

sections.title: Reformed doctrine does not differ: the dispute is about words, not the thing
sections.pass_a: LIX. From which the doctrine of the Reformed set out above does not differ, according to which they establish that all the Physical powers necessary for acting well, which are nothing else than free choice itself absolutely considered, have remained in man after sin, and that only a certain moral inability has been brought in through sin, which consists wholly in depraved habits so besetting the mind and will, that they can neither know nor love saving good, or even in the least degree advance themselves toward it, until they are freed from them through the grace of Christ. From all which it is plain, that the Protestants contradict the Roman School indeed in words, but yet in reality do not deny what the Roman School intends to affirm, and so, as we have already said, that the contention here is not about the thing itself, but about words.
pass_b: The Reformed doctrine set out above is not far from this. On it, all the physical powers needed for acting well, which are simply free choice considered absolutely, remained in man after sin.

Sin brought in only a moral inability, consisting entirely in perverse habits that so besiege mind and will that they can neither know nor love saving good, nor move themselves the least step toward it, until Christ's grace sets them free from those habits.

All this makes plain that the Protestants contradict the Roman School in words but do not in fact deny what the Roman School means to affirm. As we have already said, the dispute here is not about the thing itself but about words.

sections.title: Even in the Roman School the Protestant way of speaking is owned as Augustinian
sections.pass_a: LX. Nor yet is the manner of speaking which the Protestants use, when they say that man through sin has lost the freedom of choice, for true and saving good, so universally disapproved in the Roman School, but that men in it both celebrated and learned acknowledge it to be taken from Augustine, and agreeable to the style of scripture and of the ancient Church. Which Jansenius and his Disciples confess in good faith, as has been shown by us above.
pass_b: Yet the Protestant way of speaking, when they say that through sin man lost freedom of choice for true and saving good, is not rejected everywhere in the Roman School: famous and learned men there recognize that it is taken from Augustine and agrees with the language of Scripture and the ancient Church. Jansenius and his disciples admit this honestly, as we showed above.
